article_text:
My husband, Paddy Donnelly, who has died aged 70, was a South African who moved in the early 1980s to London. There he worked for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa (IDAF), which funded the legal costs of people tried or imprisoned for anti-apartheid activity.

In addition to its legal work, the IDAF had a large archive of photographs relating to apartheid, and Paddy ran that side of the operation, processing and distributing photos of ongoing state violence to media outlets, campaigning groups and many other organisations. He was an accomplished photographer himself, and many of his photos were held in the archive.

He had begun by taking pictures of townships and displaced people’s camps, and when he came to the UK he photographed anti-apartheid political meetings as well as visiting or exiled South African singers, musicians and activists.

Paddy was born in Germiston, south-east of Johannesburg, to parents of Irish descent: John, a bottle store manager, and Peggy (nee Sheridan), a yoga teacher. After attending the Christian Brothers school in Boksburg, near Germiston, he did national service in the Defence Force, where he avoided any serious soldiering by becoming a photographer. Afterwards he studied journalism and music at Rhodes University, Eastern Cape, before moving on to teach photography at Mafikeng College (now Mahikeng City College) in North West Province.

In his early 20s, over a two-year period, his father, mother and sister Marge all died of cancer, and after their deaths he decided to emigrate to the British Isles, first to be a photographer in Dublin and then to London, where in 1983 he joined the IDAF. We met when I visited the IDAF to source some photos for the publications section of World University Service, where I worked, and after many years together we married in 2016.

After four years at the IDAF, Paddy moved to the Catholic Agency for Overseas Development (Cafod) in London, where for more than a decade he was their media officer, also briefing photographers who were sent to record projects that the agency supported around the world. During his time with Cafod he was invited to photograph Nelson Mandela on his July 1996 visit to London as president of South Africa.

In 2006 Paddy returned to his homeland to join Africa Media Matrix, a training department for investigative journalists and documentary film-makers based at Rhodes University. He worked there until he retired in 2021, and then returned to the UK to live in York.

There he sung in the Yorkshire Bach Choir, having previously been a member of the Barts and Highbury chamber choirs in London and the Byrdsongs choir in the Eastern Cape.

He donated some of his photos and archival material to the Legacy Centre in London, a history and education hub located in the former offices of the African National Congress.

Paddy is survived by me.

EXCLUSIVE: Gregg Araki has wrapped production on his dark comedy The Decline of F*cking Western Civilization , with 12 additions rounding out a stacked cast, sources tell Deadline.

They are: Kal Penn ( Trust Me, I’m a Doctor ), Michael Chiklis ( The Senior ), David Koechner ( Anchorman ), Nat Faxon ( Loot ), Wendi McLendon-Covey ( The Goldbergs ), Steve Guttenberg ( Three Men and a Baby ), actor-producer Colleen Camp ( Euphoria ), Giovanni Ribisi ( American Hostage ), Judy Greer ( In Memoriam ), Margaret Cho ( I Want Your Sex ), Alex Borstein ( The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel ), Lulu Wilson ( Becky ), and Charlie Bushnell ( Percy Jackson and the Olympians ).

This troupe supports the previously announced Ashton Kutcher, Alison Brie, and Jesse Williams. No character details have emerged.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Gregg Araki Sets Ashton Kutcher & Alison Brie For Dark Comedy ‘The Decline of F*cking Western Civilization’; Jesse Williams In Talks

Kal Penn’s Busy Onscreen Year Includes Playing Anna Nicole Smith’s Doctor, A Gregg Araki Role & ‘Harold & Kumar 4’ In Works: “One Of The Funniest Scripts”

Little is known about the film, other than it being an ensemble piece comped as Election meets American Beauty . Production kicked off in Los Angeles in mid September.

Producers are Why Not Productions and Goodfellas. Araki is working from a script by Kevin W. Koehler, on which he’s completed revisions. The lauded indie filmmaker comes to the project on the heels of I Want You Sex , a darkly comedic erotic thriller starring Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman, which released with Magnolia Pictures this summer after premiering to critical acclaim at Sundance.

Penn is repped by UTA, Anonymous Content, and Fuller Law; Chiklis by UTA, Entertainment 360, and Ziffren Brittenham; Koechner by Gersh and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller; Faxon by CAA, Artists First, Untitled, and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman; McLendon-Covey by UTA, John Carrabino Management, and Yorn, Levine, Barnes; Guttenberg by CAA and Vault Entertainment; Camp by Gersh; Ribisi by CAA, Linden Entertainment, and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller; Greer by CAA, Artists First, and Toczek Suddleson; Cho by WME, manager Sarah J. Martin, and Fox Rothschild; Borstein by WME, The Rosenzweig Group, and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller; Wilson by UTA, Authentic, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman; and Bushnell by Vault Entertainment and Myman Greenspan Fox.

article_text:
Films and events

First Feature Competition

Fruit Gathering

Writer-director Aung Phyoe’s enthralling, visually striking drama charts a homoerotic friendship between two young Burmese women.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Aung Phyoe

With Nandar Myat Aung, Nandar Myint Lwin

Myanmar-Czechia-France 2026. 79min

Courtesy of Third Floor Production

Language Burmese With English subtitles

Introduction

San Kyi and Theint Theint Oo work in a garment factory in Yangon, formerly the capital of Myanmar. What begins as an innocent encounter between the two young women soon develops into something both delicious and dangerous. Winner of the Crystal Globe at Karlovy Vary International Film Festival, Phyoe’s rich, emotionally enveloping drama intelligently explores the complexities of the women’s relationship.

Wema Mumma

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

Contains themes of self harm.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Filipiñana

This bold debut, set over the course of one sweltering day, follows a 17-year-old working as a ‘tee-girl’ at a golf club.

Iván & Hadoum

Ian de la Rosa’s debut, set in a vast greenhouse in southern Spain, is a tender love story that finds newly promoted Iván falling for co-worker Hadoum.

Our Share of Sand

Shalini Adnani’s poignant coming-of-age drama presents a unique perspective on India’s gaping class inequality, child labour and the deep corruption underpinning a family’s economic status.

title_original: ‘I spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times’: Ron Perlman on making The Name of the Rose
editorial_title_zh: “我在肖恩·康纳利的脸上吐了16次口水”：朗·普尔曼谈《玫瑰的名字》的拍摄幕后
editorial_excerpt_zh: “当我做不出吐口水的戏份时，肖恩把我拉到一边说：‘朗，如果你不真的往我脸上吐，我们今天一整天都得耗在这儿了。’于是我吐了一口——而且不得不一遍又一遍地重拍” 我读到了一篇关于一本在意大利获得极高评价的奇特小说的文章，这是一个关于中世纪修道士为争夺亚里士多德《诗学》中虚构的缺失部分而引发的谋杀悬疑故事……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "让-雅克·阿诺（Jean-Jacques Annaud），导演", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我读到了一篇关于一本在意大利获得极高评价的奇特小说的文章，这是一个关于中世纪修道士为争夺亚里士多德《诗学》中虚构的缺失部分而引发的谋杀悬疑故事。我说：“这正合我意。”从小到大，我都对中世纪和宗教建筑着迷，而亚里士多德的《诗学》是我最喜欢的文学作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我得知原著作者翁贝托·埃科（Umberto Eco）将在法国逗留一个晚上，并同意在酒店见我，而且我还要开车送他去戴高乐机场。我第一眼看到的是他在酒店楼梯上的影子，看起来就像福尔摩斯的剪影——翁贝托是一个极具幽默感的人，他戴着猎鹿帽、嘴里叼着烟斗来见我。在车里，我问了各种问题：方济各会的修士们穿的是什么鞋？修士们留胡子吗？猪是什么颜色的？他说：“我不知道，我又没写这些东西。”最后我雇用了中世纪史学家雅克·勒戈夫（Jacques Le Goff）和他的7位同事，来确保我们在所有细节上都做到准确无误——服装、建筑、礼仪等等。", "links": [{"text": "Jacques Le Goff", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/2014/apr/24/jacques-le-goff"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想找一个不知名的演员来扮演调查这些死亡事件的修士威廉·德·巴斯克维尔（William of Baskerville），于是我走遍世界各地观看由50多岁优秀演员主演的戏剧。与此同时，经纪人迈克·奥维茨（Mike Ovitz）不断打来电话说：“肖恩·康纳利非常想拍这部电影。”终于有一天，有人敲我的门，我打开门发现肖恩夹着剧本站在那儿。他说：“听着，孩子……”然后读了起来。我起了一身鸡皮疙瘩。他念台词的方式正是我在读小说时脑海里一直听到的声音。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我飞往维也纳去观看老彼得·勃鲁盖尔（Bruegel the Elder）的画作。我想从那个时期的真实人物身上寻找灵感，那些没有牙医或医生的时代的人，不过我也挑选了一些长相不错的修士。克里斯蒂安·史莱特（Christian Slater）来为年轻的见习修士阿德索（Adso）试镜，他说：“我没背台词，我喝醉了。”选角导演玛丽·乔（Mary Jo）非常生气，试图把他赶走，但他正是我想要的人。他只有16岁，但看起来像14岁。结果证明他正是玛丽·乔的儿子。我选了3个女人来试镜村里那个没有名字的女孩的角色，但克里斯蒂安刚和维多利亚·瓦加斯（Valentina Vargas）做完银幕试镜就爱上了她，所以我再也没有见另外两个。", "links": [{"text": "Bruegel the Elder", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/jonathanjonesblog/2017/feb/09/pieter-bruegel-the-elder-holburne-museum"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们在罗马附近的山顶上为修道士和村庄搭建了一个巨大的布景。在最后图书馆高塔燃烧的那场戏中，肖恩的兜帽短暂地着火了，一块巨大的真木头砸在饰演盲僧的费奥多尔·夏利亚平（Feodor Chaliapin Jr）身上，把他撞倒在地。“我已经80岁了，”他说，“我不介意死。刚才那条拍得好吗？”他去了医院，由于他因此留下了疤痕，我们不得不调整拍摄日程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在罗马呆了4个月后，我回到了慕尼黑的制作办公室，却找不到它了。我发现电影制片人贝恩德·艾兴格（Bernd Eichinger）正把脚搭在桌上坐在地窖里。他说：“JJ，我本来不想在拍摄期间打扰你，但我把这栋楼给卖了，用来支付拍电影的费用。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4f1d4fb5da94cecc3c806e655cd0d50c5a09f3c0/258_0_3415_2732/master/3415.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "克里斯蒂安·史莱特与朗·普尔曼在《玫瑰的名字》中。", "caption": "“对于我的台词，我只是随口念道：一因、二因、三因、四因……”……朗·普尔曼与克里斯蒂安·史莱特在《玫瑰的名字》中。摄影：TCD/Prod DB/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "朗·普尔曼，饰演萨尔瓦托雷（Salvatore）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的第一部电影《火前寻爱》就是让-雅克导演的。我饰演一个穴居人。把自己变成一个完全陌生的人是一次极其有益的锻炼，也是对我进入电影界的一次非凡的引路，所以当我读到让-雅克将要执导《玫瑰的名字》时，我翻阅了小说，并发现了一个名叫萨尔瓦托雷的角色——一个智力受损、满口七种语言混杂的驼背——他将带来类似的挑战。我告诉让-雅克，这个角色将是梦想成真。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "让-雅克给了我完全的自由来构思我的台词。《玫瑰的名字》已经以80种语言出版，于是我找到了翁贝托·埃科让萨尔瓦托雷引用的那七种语言的版本，并圈出了萨尔瓦托雷开口说话的每一处。然后我就开始：“一因、二因、三因、四因——好吧，这个词是拉丁语，这个词是西班牙语，这个词是意大利语……”以此类推。这就是萨尔瓦托雷交流能力的起源。", "links": [{"text": "Umberto Eco", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/umbertoeco"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我合作了一位方言教练，他同时也是一位对该历史时期有特殊了解的历史学家。他建议了萨尔瓦托雷在被火刑柱烧死时唱的催眠曲。让-雅克有一种想法，认为萨尔瓦托雷与现实脱节得如此严重，以至于他最初甚至觉得身处那种境地很有趣。这首催眠曲传达出一种孩子般的好奇感，因为他卷入了这场仪式，却根本没有意识到自己即将失去生命。", "links": [{"text": "lullaby", "url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TXGzg3uJrOc"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我只在拍摄萨尔瓦托雷即将被由F·穆雷·亚伯拉罕（F Murray Abraham）饰演的宗教审判官伯纳多·吉（Bernardo Gui）折磨的那场戏时，戴过一次假驼峰。我在化妆椅上坐了13个多小时，等我到片场时，他们的时间几乎已经用光了。我的头发被剃光了，看起来就像得了皮肤病。他们说：“我的朋友，祝你的个人生活好运。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我尽可能抓住每一个机会和肖恩·康纳利在一起，看他演戏、听他讲故事。他是我的偶像，名不虚传。到了必须往他眼睛里吐口水的戏份时，我简直下不了手。肖恩把我拉到一旁，说道：“朗，如果你不真往我脸吐口水，我们他妈的得在这里耗上一整天。”于是我终于狠下心吐了一口。问题在于，拍摄不能只从一个角度进行，你得在侧面镜头、中景、特写、过肩镜头中反复重现……那天我肯定在肖恩·康纳利的脸上吐了16次。", article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Jean-Jacques Annaud , director"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I read an article about a curious book that had great reviews in Italy, a murder mystery about monks in the middle ages fighting for the fictional missing part of Aristotle’s Poetics. I said: “This is for me.” Since childhood, I had been fascinated with medieval and religious architecture, and Aristotle’s Poetics is my favourite literary work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I learned that Umberto Eco, the author, was going to be in France for one night and agreed to meet me at his hotel and that I would drive him to Charles de Gaulle airport. The first thing I saw was his shadow on the hotel staircase, which looked like the silhouette of Sherlock Holmes – Umberto was a man of great humour, and he met me wearing a deerstalker, with a pipe in his mouth. In the car, I asked questions: what sort of shoes would the Franciscans have been wearing? Would the monks have had beards? What colour would the pigs have been? He said: “I don’t know, I didn’t have to write any of that.” I ended up hiring medievalist Jacques Le Goff and seven of his colleagues to make sure we got all the details right – costumes, architecture, liturgy and so on.", "links": [{"text": "Jacques Le Goff", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/2014/apr/24/jacques-le-goff"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I wanted an unknown to play William of Baskerville, the friar who investigates the deaths, and travelled the world to watch plays featuring great actors in their 50s. Meanwhile, agent Mike Ovitz kept calling, saying: “Sean Connery would love to make this movie.” Eventually, there was a knock on my door and I opened it to find Sean with the screenplay under his arm. He said, “Listen, boy …” and started reading. I had goose bumps. The way he said the dialogue was exactly what I’d been hearing in my head while reading the book."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I flew to Vienna to look at paintings by Bruegel the Elder . I wanted to be inspired by the real people of the period, people who had no dentists or doctors, but I did cast some good-looking monks, too. Christian Slater turned up to audition for the young novice, Adso, and said: “I didn’t learn the lines, I got drunk.” The casting director, Mary Jo, was furious and tried to send him away, but he was the one I wanted. He was only 16, but looked 14. It turned out he was Mary Jo’s son. I had three women selected to audition for the part of the nameless girl from the village, but Christian fell in love with the first, Valentina Vargas, as soon as he did a screen test with her, so I never saw the other two.", "links": [{"text": "Bruegel the Elder", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/jonathanjonesblog/2017/feb/09/pieter-bruegel-the-elder-holburne-museum"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We built a vast set on a hilltop near Rome for the monastery and village. During the scene at the end where the library tower burns, Sean’s cowl briefly caught fire, and a big piece of real timber fell on Feodor Chaliapin Jr, who played the blind monk, knocking him to the ground. “I’m 80 years old,” he said, “I don’t mind dying. Was the take good?” He went to hospital and we had to change the schedule because he then had a scar."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "After four months in Rome, I went back to my production office in Munich and couldn’t find it. I discovered the film’s producer, Bernd Eichinger, in the cellar with his feet on a table. He said, “JJ, I didn’t want to disturb you during the shoot, but I sold the building to help pay for the movie.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4f1d4fb5da94cecc3c806e655cd0d50c5a09f3c0/258_0_3415_2732/master/3415.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Christian Slater and Ron Perlman in The Name of the Rose.", "caption": "‘For my dialogue, I just went: eenie, meenie, miny, moe’ … Ron Perlman with Christian Slater in The Name of the Rose. Photograph: TCD/Prod DB/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Ron Perlman , played Salvatore"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My very first film, Quest for Fire, was directed by Jean-Jacques. I played a caveman. Transforming myself into something completely foreign was an incredibly rewarding exercise and a phenomenal introduction to the world of cinema, so when I read that Jean-Jacques had attached himself to The Name of the Rose, I went through the book and found a character named Salvatore – an intellectually challenged hunchback who spoke in a jumble of seven languages – who would embody a similar challenge. I told Jean-Jacques that this part would be a dream come true."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jean-Jacques gave me complete freedom to figure out my dialogue. The Name of the Rose had been published in 80 languages, so I got copies in the seven that Umberto Eco has Salvatore referencing, and circled every time Salvatore spoke. Then I just went, “Eenie, meenie, miny, moe – OK, this word is Latin, this word is Spanish, this word is Italian …” and so on. That was the genesis of Salvatore’s communicative skills.", "links": [{"text": "Umberto Eco", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/umbertoeco"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I worked with a dialect coach who was also a historian with particular knowledge of the period. He suggested the lullaby that Salvatore sings when he’s burned at the stake. Jean-Jacques had this idea that Salvatore was so out of touch with reality that he was initially amused to be in that situation. The lullaby gave a sense of childlike wonder at the fact he’s involved in this ceremony, but doesn’t realise he’s about to lose his life.", "links": [{"text": "lullaby", "url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TXGzg3uJrOc"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I only had to wear the prosthetic hump once, filming the scene where Salvatore is about to be tortured by F Murray Abraham as the inquisitor, Bernardo Gui. I was in the makeup chair for more than 13 hours and by the time I got to set, they had almost run out of time. My hair was shaved so it looked like I had mange. They said: “Good luck with your personal life, my friend.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I spent every moment I could with Sean Connery, watching him act and listening to his stories. He was my hero, the real deal. When it came to the scene where I had to spit in his eye, I just couldn’t do it. article_text:
Jean-Jacques Annaud , director

I read an article about a curious book that had great reviews in Italy, a murder mystery about monks in the middle ages fighting for the fictional missing part of Aristotle’s Poetics. I said: “This is for me.” Since childhood, I had been fascinated with medieval and religious architecture, and Aristotle’s Poetics is my favourite literary work.

I learned that Umberto Eco, the author, was going to be in France for one night and agreed to meet me at his hotel and that I would drive him to Charles de Gaulle airport. The first thing I saw was his shadow on the hotel staircase, which looked like the silhouette of Sherlock Holmes – Umberto was a man of great humour, and he met me wearing a deerstalker, with a pipe in his mouth. In the car, I asked questions: what sort of shoes would the Franciscans have been wearing? Would the monks have had beards? What colour would the pigs have been? He said: “I don’t know, I didn’t have to write any of that.” I ended up hiring medievalist Jacques Le Goff and seven of his colleagues to make sure we got all the details right – costumes, architecture, liturgy and so on.

I wanted an unknown to play William of Baskerville, the friar who investigates the deaths, and travelled the world to watch plays featuring great actors in their 50s. Meanwhile, agent Mike Ovitz kept calling, saying: “Sean Connery would love to make this movie.” Eventually, there was a knock on my door and I opened it to find Sean with the screenplay under his arm. He said, “Listen, boy …” and started reading. I had goose bumps. The way he said the dialogue was exactly what I’d been hearing in my head while reading the book.

I flew to Vienna to look at paintings by Bruegel the Elder . I wanted to be inspired by the real people of the period, people who had no dentists or doctors, but I did cast some good-looking monks, too. Christian Slater turned up to audition for the young novice, Adso, and said: “I didn’t learn the lines, I got drunk.” The casting director, Mary Jo, was furious and tried to send him away, but he was the one I wanted. He was only 16, but looked 14. It turned out he was Mary Jo’s son. I had three women selected to audition for the part of the nameless girl from the village, but Christian fell in love with the first, Valentina Vargas, as soon as he did a screen test with her, so I never saw the other two.

We built a vast set on a hilltop near Rome for the monastery and village. During the scene at the end where the library tower burns, Sean’s cowl briefly caught fire, and a big piece of real timber fell on Feodor Chaliapin Jr, who played the blind monk, knocking him to the ground. “I’m 80 years old,” he said, “I don’t mind dying. Was the take good?” He went to hospital and we had to change the schedule because he then had a scar.

After four months in Rome, I went back to my production office in Munich and couldn’t find it. I discovered the film’s producer, Bernd Eichinger, in the cellar with his feet on a table. He said, “JJ, I didn’t want to disturb you during the shoot, but I sold the building to help pay for the movie.”

Ron Perlman , played Salvatore

My very first film, Quest for Fire, was directed by Jean-Jacques. I played a caveman. Transforming myself into something completely foreign was an incredibly rewarding exercise and a phenomenal introduction to the world of cinema, so when I read that Jean-Jacques had attached himself to The Name of the Rose, I went through the book and found a character named Salvatore – an intellectually challenged hunchback who spoke in a jumble of seven languages – who would embody a similar challenge. I told Jean-Jacques that this part would be a dream come true.

Jean-Jacques gave me complete freedom to figure out my dialogue. The Name of the Rose had been published in 80 languages, so I got copies in the seven that Umberto Eco has Salvatore referencing, and circled every time Salvatore spoke. Then I just went, “Eenie, meenie, miny, moe – OK, this word is Latin, this word is Spanish, this word is Italian …” and so on. That was the genesis of Salvatore’s communicative skills.

I worked with a dialect coach who was also a historian with particular knowledge of the period. He suggested the lullaby that Salvatore sings when he’s burned at the stake. Jean-Jacques had this idea that Salvatore was so out of touch with reality that he was initially amused to be in that situation. The lullaby gave a sense of childlike wonder at the fact he’s involved in this ceremony, but doesn’t realise he’s about to lose his life.

I only had to wear the prosthetic hump once, filming the scene where Salvatore is about to be tortured by F Murray Abraham as the inquisitor, Bernardo Gui. I was in the makeup chair for more than 13 hours and by the time I got to set, they had almost run out of time. My hair was shaved so it looked like I had mange. They said: “Good luck with your personal life, my friend.”

I spent every moment I could with Sean Connery, watching him act and listening to his stories. He was my hero, the real deal. When it came to the scene where I had to spit in his eye, I just couldn’t do it. Sean took me aside, and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all fucking day.” So I finally just let one fly. The problem was, you don’t film from just one angle, you have to recreate in profile, medium shot, closeup, over-the-shoulder … I must have spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times that day.

Other Oscar nominations : Adapted Screenplay Wins : Adapted Screenplay The scene that proves it : “What if they’re not guilty?” A winner for best adapted screenplay, making Polley the fourth lone woman writer to win this category after Siân Heder for “CODA” (2021), Emma Thompson for “Sense and Sensibility” (1995) and Ruth Prawer Jhabvala, who won twice for “Howard’s End” (1993) and “A Room with a View” (1986)."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Women-Talking.jpg?w=300", "alt": "Women Talking", "caption": "Image Credit: Courtesy of United Artists Releasing", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Anatomy of a Fall (2023) Image Credit: Neon Justine Triet Film : “Anatomy of a Fall” Distributed by : Neon Written by : Justine Triet, Arthur Harari Produced by : Marie-Ange Luciani and David Thion Synopsis : A woman is suspected of murder after her husband’s death, and their visually challenged son faces a moral dilemma as the main witness. Other Oscar nominations : director, actress (Sandra Hüller), original screenplay, film editing (Laurent Sénéchal) Wins : Best Original Screenplay (Justine Triet and Arthur Harari) The scene that proves it : “Sometimes a couple is kind of a chaos and everybody is lost. Sometimes we fight together and sometimes we fight alone, and sometimes we fight against each other, that happens.” Triet is the second female director nominated for a non-English language film after Lina Wertmüller for “Seven Beauties” (1976) and the seventh female nominated for directing and writing the same movie."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Anatomy-of-a-Fall.jpg?w=300", "alt": "Anatomy of a Fall", "caption": "Image Credit: Neon", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Barbie (2023) Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection Greta Gerwig Film : “Barbie” Distributed by : Warner Bros. Written by : Greta Gerwig and Noah Baumbach (based on ‘Barbie’ by Mattel) Produced by : David Heyman, Margot Robbie, Tom Ackerley, Robbie Brenner Synopsis : Barbie and Ken are having the time of their lives in the colorful and seemingly perfect world of Barbie Land. However, when they get a chance to go to the real world, they soon discover the joys and perils of living among humans. Other Oscar nominations : supporting actor (Ryan Gosling), supporting actress (America Ferrera), adapted screenplay, production design (Sarah Greenwood, Katie Spencer), costume design (Jacqueline Durran), original song (“I’m Just Ken” by Mark Ronson and Andrew Wyatt and “What Was I Made For?” by Billie Eilish and Finneas O’Connell) Wins : Original Song (“What Was I Made For?” by Billie Eilish and Finneas O’Connell) The scene that proves it : “It is literally impossible to be a woman.” Gerwig’s summer blockbuster hit made over $1.4 billion globally, making it the highest-grossing best picture nominee helmed by a female director. In addition, she’s the first director in history to have their first three solo directorial features nominated for best picture, in addition to “Lady Bird” (2017) and “Little Women” (2019), and the only woman to helm three best picture nominees."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/MCDBARB_WB112-e1706285503100.jpg?w=300", "alt": "BARBIE, from left: America Ferrera, Ariana Greenblatt, Margot Robbie, 2023. © Warner Bos. / Courtesy Everett Collection", "caption": "Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Past Lives (2023) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection Celine Song Film : “Past Lives” Distributed by : A24 Written by : Celine Song Produced by : David Hinojosa, Christine Vachon, Pamela Koffler Synopsis : Nora and Hae Sung, two deeply connected childhood friends, are wrested apart after Nora’s family emigrates from South Korea. Twenty years later, they are reunited for one fateful week as they confront notions of love and destiny. Other Oscar nominations : original screenplay Wins : None The scene that proves it : “You make my world so much bigger and I’m wondering if I do the same for you?” Song is the first woman of color to helm a best picture nominated movie with her directorial debut."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Greatest-Love-Stories-Past-Lives.jpg?w=300", "alt": "PAST LIVES, from left: Teo YOO, Greta Lee, John Magro, 2023. © A24 / Courtesy Everett Collection", "caption": "Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The Substance (2024) Image Credit: Christine Tamalet Coralie Fargeat Film : “The Substance” Distributed by : Mubi Written by : Coralie Fargeat Produced by : Coralie Fargeat, Tim Bevan, and Eric Fellner Synopsis : A fading celebrity takes a black-market drug: a cell-replicating substance that creates a younger, better version of herself. Other Oscar nominations : director, actress (Demi Moore), original screenplay, and makeup and hairstyling Wins : Makeup and Hairstyling (Pierre-Olivier Persin, Stéphanie Guillon, and Marilyne Scarselli) The scene that proves it : Putting on lipstick in front of the mirror. Fargeat is the ninth woman to receive a directing bid at the Academy Awards, with the eight other female filmmakers"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Substance_7b58d1.jpg?w=300", "alt": "The SUBSTANCE (2024) Demi Moore Credit: Mubi", "caption": "Image Credit: Christine Tamalet", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Hamnet (2025) Image Credit: Agata Grzybowska Chloé Zhao Film : “Hamnet” Distributed by : Focus Features Written by : Chloé Zhao and Maggie O’Farrell (based on the novel “Hamnet” by Maggie O’Farrell) Produced by : Liza Marshall, Pippa Harris, Nicolas Gonda, Steven Spielberg, Sam Mendes Synopsis : In late 16th-century England, Agnes, a healer sensitive to the world around her, builds a home with William, a local tutor and aspiring playwright. As their lives fracture, they are tested by distance, silence, and grief. Other Oscar nominations : director, actress (Jessie Buckley), adapted screenplay, casting (Nina Gold), production design (Fiona Crombie and Alice Felton) and costume design (Malgosia Turzanska) Wins : Best Actress (Jessie Buckley) The scene that proves it : Watching “Hamlet” at the Globe Theatre Zhao is the second woman to be nominated for directing more than once, after Jane Campion."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Jessie-Buckley-Hamnet.jpg?w=300", "alt": "Jessie Buckley Hamnet", "caption": "Image Credit: Agata Grzybowska", "credit": "Variety · Film"}]
article_text:
Across the history of the Academy Awards, hundreds of films have been nominated for the top prize, best picture. Only a small fraction of them were helmed by a woman director. The disparity is startling, even as female-led stories continue to gain ground.

Women filmmakers are taking the reins in Hollywood, with many stepping behind the camera to tell stories that reach global audiences. Recognition for that talent at the Oscars, though, has been slow to follow, especially in the best director category. In most years, only a handful of best picture nominees and sometimes none at all, are directed by women, even as the number of female producers behind nominated films has steadily climbed.

When breakthroughs come, they tend to arrive as firsts: the women who crack the directing race, the producers who make history by nationality or background and the rare repeat winners. Below, we track those milestones and the films that carried them.

Here is the complete, continually updated list of every woman-directed film nominated for the Oscars’ top prize, best picture.

Variety Awards Circuit: Oscars

Children of a Lesser God (1986) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Randa Haines Film : “Children of a Lesser God” (1986) Distributed by : Paramount Pictures Written by : Hesper Anderson, Mark Medoff (based on “Children of a Lesser God” by Mark Medoff Produced by : Burt Sugarman, Patrick J. Palmer Synopsis : A new speech teacher at a school for the deaf falls in love with the janitor, a deaf woman speechless by choice. Other Oscar nominations : actor (William Hurt), actress (Marlee Matlin), supporting actress (Piper Laurie) and adapted screenplay Wins : Marlee Matlin for best actress – first deaf person to win an acting Oscar, and youngest woman to win at 21. The scene that proves it : “Never come inside my silence.” The first film directed by a woman to be nominated for best picture came at the 59th ceremony, with debut director Randa Haines. However, she was not among the five nominated men in her respective lineup that included winner Oliver Stone (“Platoon”), David Lynch (“Blue Velvet”), James Ivory (“A Room with a View”), Roland Joffé (“The Mission”) and Woody Allen (“Hannah and Her Sisters”). The recognition came three years after Barbra Streisand came up short with “Yentl” (1983) after winning the Golden Globe for directing and best picture (comedy or musical). “Children of a Lesser God” received multiple accolades including a DGA nom for Haines and the Silver Bear at the Berlin Film Festival. Haines has directed three other feature films following her historic recognition – “The Doctor” (1991), “Wrestling Ernest Hemingway” (1993) and “Dance with Me” (1998). Her last directorial credit is for television movie “The Ron Clark Story” (2006).

Awakenings (1990) Image Credit: ©Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Penny Marshall Film : “Awakenings” (1990) Distributed by : Columbia Pictures Written by : Steven Zaillian (based on “Awakenings” by Oliver Sacks) Produced by : Walter F. Parkes, Lawrence Lasker Synopsis : The victims of an encephalitis epidemic many years ago have been catatonic ever since, but now a new drug offers the prospect of reviving them. Other Oscar nominations : actor (Robert DeNiro) and adapted screenplay Wins : None The scene that proves it : “The drugs not working.” Penny Marshall’s powerful drama that’s based on the 1973 memoir beat incredible odds to make the lineup of the 63rd Academy Awards best picture lineup that included “Ghost,” “The Godfather Part III,” “Goodfellas” and eventual winner “Dances with Wolves.” The movie itself didn’t receive any best picture nominations from any major awards bodies, and even DeNiro’s nom was a surprise considering the Golden Globes had cited Robin Williams. What’s most unfortunate about the “Laverne & Shirley” star is she left us without any formal Oscar recognition during her outstanding career as a filmmaker. “Awakenings” is the only one of her seven directorial features to be nominated, despite helming classics like “Big” (1988) and “A League of Their Own” (1992).

The Prince of Tides (1991) Image Credit: ©Columbia Pictures/courtesy Everett Co / Everett Collection Barbra Streisand Film : “The Prince of Tides” Distributed by : Columbia Pictures Written by : Pat Conroy, Becky Johnston (based on the novel “The Prince of Tides” by Pat Conroy) Produced by : Barbra Streisand, Andrew S. Karsch Synopsis : A troubled man talks to his suicidal sister’s psychiatrist about their family history and falls in love with her in the process. Other Oscar nominations : actor (Nick Nolte), supporting actress (Kate Nelligan), adapted screenplay, cinematography (Stephen Goldblatt), production design (Paul Sylbert, Caryl Heller) and original score (James Newton Howard) Wins : None The scene that proves it : “I didn’t know it could happen to a boy” Academy Award winner Barbra Streisand has shown she has the acting chops with her best actress win for “Funny Girl” (1968) and nom for “The Way We Were” (1973), along with her songwriting abilities with her win for original song for the chart-topper “Evergreen” from “A Star is Born” (1976), which she co-wrote with Paul Williams. After becoming the first woman to win a Golden Globe for directing “Yentl” (1983), but ultimately coming up short at the Oscars, she returned in a significant way with “The Prince of Tides,” the adaptation of the novel by Pat Conroy, and at the 64th ceremony, was the most nominated movie directed by a woman (at the time). Despite landing her first DGA nomination for directing, she was omitted from the directing category in favor of eventual winner Jonathan Demme (“The Silence of the Lambs”), Barry Levinson (“Bugsy”), John Singleton (“Boyz n the Hood”), Oliver Stone (“JFK”) and Ridley Scott (“Thelma & Louise”). She became the first woman to be nominated as a producer, for a film that she also directed.

The Piano (1993) Image Credit: ©Miramax/Courtesy Everett Collection Jane Campion Film : “The Piano” Distributed by : Miramax Films Written by : Jane Campion Produced by : Jan Chapman Synopsis : In the mid-19th century, a mute woman is sent to New Zealand along with her young daughter and prized piano for an arranged marriage to a wealthy landowner, but is soon lusted after by a local worker on the plantation. Other Oscar nominations : director, actress (Holly Hunter), supporting actress (Anna Paquin), original screenplay, cinematography (Stuart Dryburgh), costume design (Janet Patterson) and film editing (Veronika Jenet) Wins : actress, supporting actress and original screenplay The scene that proves it : “I trusted you.” (trigger warning for film clip) Jane Campion became the second woman to be nominated for directing after the legendary trailblazer Lina Wertmüller for “Seven Beauties” (1975), and the first woman to be nominated in picture, directing and screenplay categories in the same year. Likely the runner-up to eventual best picture winner and director “Schindler’s List” from Steven Spielberg, the New Zealand-born auteur went on to helm four other projects that didn’t land on Oscar’s radar in a substantial way – “The Portrait of a Lady” (1996), “Holy Smoke” (1999), “In the Cut” (2003) and “Bright Star” (2009). It would be 12 years before the master filmmaker would return with her dark western adaptation of the novel “The Power of the Dog,” that landed 12 Oscar nominations, the most for any film directed by a woman.

Lost in Translation (2003) Image Credit: ©Focus Films/Courtesy Everett Collection Sofia Coppola Film : “Lost in Translation” Distributed by : Focus Features Written by : Sofia Coppola Produced by : Ross Katz, Sofia Coppola Synopsis : A faded movie star and a neglected young woman form an unlikely bond after crossing paths in Tokyo. Other Oscar nominations : director, actor (Bill Murray) and original screenplay Wins : Original screenplay The scene that proves it : Bob whispers in Charlotte’s ear after saying goodbye. Sofia Coppola became the first woman to be nominated for writing, directing, and producing in the same year and the first American woman recognized for best director. She’s also one of five female scribes to be the sole writer for a winner in original screenplay after Frances Marion (“The Big House” and “The Champ”), Callie Khouri (“Thelma & Louise”), Jane Campion (“The Piano”), Diablo Cody (“Juno”) and Emerald Fennell (“Promising Young Woman”). For cinephiles, “Lost in Translation” wasn’t the beginning of our love for Coppola. Before winning her Oscar, she made her feature directorial debut with the coming-of-age drama “The Virgin Suicides” (1999). Afterward, she’s helmed the historical drama “Marie Antoinette” (2006), the contemporary crime film “The Bling Ring” (2013) and the remake of “The Beguiled” (2017), which she won best director at the Cannes Film Festival, becoming the second woman in the festival’s history to win the award. Her most recent film was “On the Rocks” (2020), which reunited her with Murray.

Little Miss Sunshine (2006) Image Credit: ©Fox Searchlight/Courtesy Everett Collection Valerie Faris Also directed by : Jonathan Dayton Film : “Little Miss Sunshine” Distributed by : Fox Searchlight Pictures (now Searchlight Pictures) Written by : Michael Arndt Produced by : David T. Friendly, Peter Saraf, Marc Turtletaub Synopsis : A family determined to get their young daughter into the finals of a beauty pageant take a cross-country trip in their VW bus. Other Oscar nominations : supporting actor (Alan Arkin), supporting actress (Abigail Breslin) and original screenplay Wins : supporting actor and original screenplay The scene that proves it : “Why would you want to kill yourself?” The classic dramedy marks the feature film directorial debut from husband-and-wife team Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris, best known for their innovative music video visions working with artists like R.E.M., Oasis and The Smashing Pumpkins. After premiering at the Sundance Film Festival, the movie was a box office hit, earning over $100 million on an $8 million budget, receiving critical acclaim but missing out on a nom for directing for the couple. Up to that point in Oscar history, only “West Side Story” (1961) directors Robert Wise and Jerome Robbins were able to win for a shared directing credit. The other nominees were eventual winner Martin Scorsese (“The Departed”), Alejandro G. Iñárritu (“Babel”), Clint Eastwood (“Letters from Iwo Jima”), Paul Greengrass (“United 93”) and Stephen Frears (“The Queen”). An easy argument can be made that the film was second to “The Departed” in best picture after winning the Producers Guild of America and Screen Actors Guild Awards’ top prizes. In addition, Faris is the only woman to direct a cast to an ensemble win at the SAG Awards.

The Hurt Locker (2009) Image Credit: Summit Entertainment/courtesy Everett Collection Kathryn Bigelow Film : “The Hurt Locker” Distributed by : Summit Entertainment Written by : Mark Boal Produced by : Kathryn Bigelow, Mark Boal, Nicolas Chartier, Greg Shapiro Synopsis : During the Iraq War, a Sergeant recently assigned to an army bomb squad is put at odds with his squad mates due to his maverick way of handling his work. Other Oscar nominations : director, actor (Jeremy Renner), original screenplay, cinematography (Barry Ackroyd), film editing (Bob Murawski, Chris Innis), sound mixing (Paul N.J. Ottosson, Ray Beckett), sound editing (Paul N.J. Ottosson) and original score (Marco Beltrami, Buck Sanders) Wins : picture, director, original screenplay, film editing, sound mixing and sound editing The scene that proves it : “I got a wire.” Kathryn Bigelow made history as the first woman to win best director for her best picture-winning war drama, “The Hurt Locker,” when a woman-directed feature led the nomination tally, a first-ever. It’s also the most Oscar won by a best picture winner since the field has expanded from five to 10 (other films like “Gravity” and “Mad Max: Fury Road” have also won the same or more but did not win picture). Despite being one of the lowest box-office-winning films in history, Bigelow also became the first woman to win the DGA award. The film grossed $49 million on a $15 million budget. Before becoming an Oscar-winner, movie lovers were well-aware of Bigelow’s talents with films like “Near Dark” (1987), “Blue Steel” (1990), “Point Break” (1991) and “Strange Days” (1995) among her finest efforts. After her winning year, she got another film in the Oscars’ top category, “Zero Dark Thirty” (2012), one of the few films that won best film at New York, Los Angeles and National Board of Review awards. After that, she directed “Detroit” (2017), receiving mixed praise from critics but still showcasing her eye for tension. We await the next adventure.

An Education (2009) Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Lone Scherfig Film : “An Education” Distributed by : Sony Pictures Classics Written by : Nick Hornby (based on “An Education” by Lynn Barber) Produced by : Finola Dwyer and Amanda Posey Synopsis : “A coming-of-age story about a teenage girl in 1960s suburban London, and how her life changes with the arrival of a playboy nearly twice her age.” Other Oscar nominations : actress (Carey Mulligan) and adapted screenplay Wins : None The scene that proves it : “This is the one Danny.” The Hollywood arrival of Carey Mulligan is one of the most memorable of the 2009 cinematic year, and that’s thanks to director Lone Scherfig, who helmed the coming-of-age drama “An Education.” The British film also is a major part of Academy history as the first time that two films helmed by women filmmakers were nominated for best picture, along with the eventual winner “The Hurt Locker” from Kathryn Bigelow. Since her acclaimed film, Scherfig has been behind smaller projects like “One Day” (2011), “The Riot Club” (2014), “Their Finest” (2016) and “The Kindness of Strangers” (2019). She’s attached to direct “The Movie Teller” with Daniel Bruhl and Berence Bejo for her next project.

The Kids Are All Right (2010) Image Credit: ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection Lisa Cholodenko Film : “The Kids Are All Right” Distributed by : Focus Features Written by : Lisa Cholodenko, Stuart Blumberg Produced by : Gary Gilbert, Jeffrey Kusama-Hinte, Celine Rattray Synopsis : Two children conceived by artificial insemination bring their biological father into their non-traditional family life. Other Oscar nominations : actress (Annette Bening), supporting actor (Mark Ruffalo) and original screenplay Wins : None The scene that proves it : “I need to say something.” Lisa Cholodenko’s honest and raw look at a same-sex couple raising two teenagers is one of the most underrated in the canon of the best women-directed features. What she’s able to pull out of her stars Annette Bening and Mark Ruffalo, who received Oscar nominations, and Julianne Moore, who was egregiously snubbed, is nothing short of remarkable. Also, part of a year that saw two female-led films nominated for best picture, the dramedy is rich and full moments and gained multiple accolades.

Winter’s Bone (2010) Image Credit: ©Roadside Attractions/Courtesy Everett Collection Debra Granik Film : “Winter’s Bone Distributed by : Roadside Attractions Written by : Debra Granik, Anne Rossellini (based on the novel “Winter’s Bone” by Daniel Woodrell) Produced by : Anne Rossellini, Alix Madigan Synopsis : An unflinching Ozark Mountain girl hacks through dangerous social terrain as she hunts down her drug-dealing father while trying to keep her family intact. Other Oscar nominations : actress (Jennifer Lawrence), supporting actor (John Hawkes) and adapted screenplay Wins : None The scene that proves it : “She ain’t my brother.” Writer and director Debra Granik allowed the world to know and fall in love with stars Jennifer Lawrence and John Hawkes, who earned nominations for their performances in the Sundance Film Festival standout. Receiving multiple accolades, the film was brushed by Ben Affleck’s sophomore effort, “The Town,” and landed a best picture nomination. Unfortunately, Granik wasn’t nominated for directing to the dismay of critics.

Zero Dark Thirty (2012) Image Credit: ©Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Kathryn Bigelow Film : “Zero Dark Thirty” Distributed by : Sony Pictures Written by : Mark Boal Produced by : Mark Boal, Kathryn Bigelow, Megan Ellison Synopsis : A chronicle of the decade-long hunt for al-Qaeda terrorist leader Osama bin Laden after the September 2001 attacks and his death at the hands of the Navy S.E.A.L.s Team 6 in May 2011. Other Oscar nominations : actress (Jessica Chastain), original screenplay, film editing (William Goldenberg, Dylan Tichenor) and sound editing (Paul N.J. Ottoson) Wins : sound editing (tied with “Skyfall”) The scene that proves it : “You must be pretty important, you have the whole plane to yourself. Where do you want to go?” Kathryn Bigelow’s follow-up, in many ways, is even more compelling than her best picture winner “The Hurt Locker” (2010). Under the incredible performance of Jessica Chastain, the true story of the hunt for terrorist Osama Bin Laden is one of the most suspenseful efforts in the last decade. However, in what many believe is the product of dirty campaign tactics, the film came up empty in best director for Bigelow despite nominations from the DGA and BAFTA. Nevertheless, the scenes that depict the SEALs gaining entry into the compound are masterfully executed, thanks to the crisp camerawork and Bigelow’s firm hand.

Selma (2014) Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection / Everett Collection Ava DuVernay Film : “Selma” Distributed by : Paramount Pictures Written by : Paul Webb Produced by : Christian Colson, Oprah Winfrey, Dede Gardner, Jeremy Kleiner Synopsis : A chronicle of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.’s campaign to secure equal voting rights via an epic march from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, in 1965. Other Oscar nominations : original song (“Glory” written by Common and John Legend) Wins : Original song The scene that proves it : “If I asked you something, would you answer me with the truth?” Ava DuVernay’s beautiful and honest depiction of the historic march in 1965 from Selma to Montogomery for voting rights is a staple in Oscars history. It stands as the first feature directed by a Black woman to be nominated for best picture. As one of the producers, Oprah Winfrey became the first Black woman to be nominated for best picture. She’s also one of three women to have two career nominations for producing and acting, with her past mention for “The Color Purple” (1985) in supporting actress. In addition, co-songwriter John Legend became an EGOT after winning original song for the hit song “Glory.” DuVernay’s place in the best director lineup didn’t come to fruition despite mentions at the Golden Globes. She missed out in favor of eventual winner Alejandro G. Iñárritu (“The Revenant”), Bennett Miller (“Foxcatcher”), Morten Tyldum (“The Imitation Game”), Richard Linklater (“Boyhood”) and Wes Anderson (“The Grand Budapest Hotel”).

Lady Bird (2017) Image Credit: Courtesy of A24 Greta Gerwig Film : “Lady Bird” Distributed by : A24 Written by : Greta Gerwig Produced by : Scott Rudin, Eli Bush, Evelyn O’Neill Synopsis : In 2002, an artistically inclined seventeen-year-old girl comes of age in Sacramento, California. Other Oscar nominations : director, actress (Saoirse Ronan), supporting actress (Laurie Metcalf), original screenplay Wins : None The scene that proves it : “Let’s just sit with what we heard.” Greta Gerwig’s first solo outing as a director, with her hilarious and moving “Lady Bird,” is a staple of the decade. Landing a possible career-best from Saoirse Ronan, who won the Golden Globe, and the critical darling of the respective season Laurie Metcalf, won the most prizes for supporting actress. Gerwig’s inclusion in the best director lineup is substantial, not just based on her inclusion, but for the entire makeup of the category that included eventual winner and Latino visionary Guillermo del Toro (“The Shape of Water”), sci-fi master Christopher Nolan (“Dunkirk”), horror-comedy extraordinaire and eventual winner of original screenplay Jordan Peele (“Get Out”) and master auteur Paul Thomas Anderson (“Phantom Thread”). The actress-turned-director shows no signs of stopping, and we should be grateful for the opportunity to witness her brilliance.

Little Women (2019) Image Credit: Sony Pictures Greta Gerwig Film : “Little Women” Distributed by : Sony Pictures Written by : Greta Gerwig (based on “Little Woman” by Louisa May Alcott) Produced by : Amy Pascal Synopsis : Jo March reflects back and forth on her life, telling the beloved story of the March sisters – four young women, each determined to live life on her own terms. Other Oscar nominations : actress (Saoirse Ronan), supporting actress (Florence Pugh), adapted screenplay, costume design (Jacqueline Durran), original score (Alexandre Desplat) Wins : Costume design The scene that proves it : “Beth’s last Christmas” Greta Gerwig, who’s also one of our finest actresses with outstanding turns in films like “20th Century Women” and “Frances Ha,” is one of the few to have nominated two best picture nominees over her career, and has done it in the shortest amount of time between “Lady Bird” (2017) and the remake of “Little Women” (2019). Her next outing will be a live-action feature version of “Barbie” starring Margot Robbie, based on the popular children’s doll.

Nomadland (2020) Image Credit: Courtesy Searchlight Chloé Zhao Film : “Nomadland” Distributed by : Searchlight Pictures Written by : Chloé Zhao (based on “Nomadland: Surviving America in the Twenty-First Century” by Jessica Bruder) Produced by : Frances McDormand, Peter Spears, Mollye Asher, Dan Janvey, Chloé Zhao Synopsis : A woman in her sixties, after losing everything in the Great Recession, embarks on a journey through the American West, living as a van-dwelling modern-day nomad. Other Oscar nominations : directing, actress (Frances McDormand), adapted screenplay, cinematography (Joshua James Richards) and editing (Chloé Zhao) Wins : picture, director and actress. Zhao became the second woman to direct an Oscar-winner for best picture and the first woman of color to be nominated and win. McDormand was the first woman to be nominated for producing and acting in the same year and the first person to win an acting award when nominated for both. The scene that proves it : “How can I be alive on this Earth, when he’s not?” With her nominations for picture, director, adapted screenplay and editing, Chloé Zhao became the first woman to score four noms in a single year, and the ninth person ever to achieve it after Warren Beatty (twice), Alfonso Cuaron, Joel Coen & Ethan Coen, Alan Menken, Francis Ford Coppola, Orson Welles and Walt Disney. In addition, “Nomadland” became the second film directed by a woman to win best picture. Since her achievement, Zhao co-wrote and directed Marvel’s “Eternals” (2021).

Promising Young Woman (2020) Image Credit: Merie Weismiller Wallace; SMPSP Emerald Fennell Film : “Promising Young Woman” Distributed by : Focus Features Written by : Emerald Fennell Produced by : Ben Browning, Ashley Fox, Emerald Fennell, Josey McNamara Synopsis : A young woman, traumatized by a tragic event in her past, seeks out vengeance against those who crossed her path. Other Oscar nominations : director, actress (Carey Mulligan), original screenplay and film editing (Frédéric Thoraval) Wins : Original screenplay The scene that proves it : “I forgive you.” Emerald Fennell, a first-time director, was nominated for picture, director and screenplay, the third woman at the time to achieve this feat. She’s also one of five female scribes to be the sole writer on a winner for original screenplay after Frances Marion (“The Big House” and “The Champ”), Callie Khouri (“Thelma & Louise”), Jane Campion (“The Piano”), Sofia Coppola (“Lost in Translation”) and Diablo Cody (“Juno”).

CODA (2021) Image Credit: Sundance Siân Heder Film : “CODA” Distributed by : Apple Original Films Written by : Siân Heder (based on the 2014 French film, “La Famille Bélier” from Éric Lartigau) Produced by : Philippe Rousselet, Fabrice Gianfermi and Patrick Wachsberger Synopsis : As a CODA (Child of Deaf Adults) Ruby is the only hearing person in her deaf family. When the family’s fishing business is threatened, Ruby finds herself torn between pursuing her love of music by wanting to go to Berklee College of Music and her fear of abandoning her parents. Other Oscar nominations : supporting actor (Troy Kotsur) and adapted screenplay Wins : best picture, supporting actor (Troy Kotsur), adapted screenplay (Siân Heder) The scene that proves it : Ruby singing “You’re All I Need to Get By” Directed and written by Oscar nominee Siân Heder, “CODA” has captured the hearts of many industry voters. Starting its journey at the Sundance Film Festival in January 2020, where it was purchased for a record-setting $25 million, the film has generated a slow but steady rise in buzz and projections. Heder is also the second woman to direct a cast to an ensemble win at the Screen Actors Guild Awards, following Valerie Faris for “Little Miss Sunshine” (2006). She was the tenth woman to direct a nominated ensemble. “CODA” won best picture and is the second film to win without a DGA mention (behind “Driving Miss Daisy”) and the second film in history to win without any below-the-line nominations behind “Grand Hotel” (1932). Heder won adapted screenplay and is the third lone woman to win this category after Emma Thompson for “Sense and Sensibility” (1995) and Ruth Prawer Jhabvala, who won twice for “Howard’s End” (1993) and “A Room with a View” (1986).

The Power of the Dog (2021) Image Credit: Courtesy of Kirsty Griffin/Netflix Jane Campion Film : “The Power of the Dog” Distributed by : Netflix Written by : Jane Campion Produced by : Jane Campion, Tanya Seghatchian, Emile Sherman, Iain Canning and Roger Frappie Synopsis : Charismatic rancher Phil Burbank inspires fear and awe in those around him. She’s also only the fourth woman to score three nods in a single year after Sofia Coppola (“Lost in Translation”), Fran Walsh (“The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King”) and Emerald Fennell (“Promising Young Woman”). Chloé Zhao (“Nomadland”) made history with four noms in 2021. She is the third woman to win best director.

Women Talking (2022) Image Credit: Courtesy of United Artists Releasing Sarah Polley Film : “Women Talking” Distributed by : MGM/United Artists Releasing Written by : Sarah Polley Produced by : Dede Gardner, Jeremy Kleiner, Frances McDormand Synopsis : Do nothing. Other Oscar nominations : Adapted Screenplay Wins : Adapted Screenplay The scene that proves it : “What if they’re not guilty?” A winner for best adapted screenplay, making Polley the fourth lone woman writer to win this category after Siân Heder for “CODA” (2021), Emma Thompson for “Sense and Sensibility” (1995) and Ruth Prawer Jhabvala, who won twice for “Howard’s End” (1993) and “A Room with a View” (1986).

Anatomy of a Fall (2023) Image Credit: Neon Justine Triet Film : “Anatomy of a Fall” Distributed by : Neon Written by : Justine Triet, Arthur Harari Produced by : Marie-Ange Luciani and David Thion Synopsis : A woman is suspected of murder after her husband’s death, and their visually challenged son faces a moral dilemma as the main witness. Barbie (2023) Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection Greta Gerwig Film : “Barbie” Distributed by : Warner Bros. Written by : Greta Gerwig and Noah Baumbach (based on ‘Barbie’ by Mattel) Produced by : David Heyman, Margot Robbie, Tom Ackerley, Robbie Brenner Synopsis : Barbie and Ken are having the time of their lives in the colorful and seemingly perfect world of Barbie Land. article_text:
Artículos

Cartelera Cinemex – Estrenos de películas 29 de octubre, 2026

Por: Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás esta semana?

Ya sea que tengas ganas de una historia emotiva, un thriller intenso o puro entretenimiento para desconectarte, los nuevos lanzamientos de películas en la cartelera Cinemex ofrecen opciones para todos los gustos.

Aquí te contamos cuáles son las películas que llegan a la cartelera Cinemex esta semana y la siguiente. Una guía rápida para decidir qué ver, cuándo ir y no perderte los títulos más comentados del momento.

Cartelera Cinemex: estrenos del jueves 29 de octubre de 2026

Sensatez y sentimiento (Sense and Sensibility) / Dir.a Georgia Oakley / Reino Unido, EE. UU. / 2026

El último gran golpe (The Get Out) / Dir. Derrick Borte / EE. UU., Australia / 2026 El propietario de un club nocturno está a punto de dejar atrás su peligroso pasado para jubilarse. Después de que hombres armados enmascarados le roban y se ve oprimido por cárteles despiadados, llega un misterioso recién llegado interesado en comprar el negocio.

Sensatez y sentimiento (Sense and Sensibility) / Dir.a Georgia Oakley / Reino Unido, EE. UU. / 2026 Tres hermanas experimentan el amor y el desamor tras verse obligadas a abandonar la finca familiar con su madre viuda y mudarse a una humilde cabaña.

Ciudad de muertos / Dir. J.M Cravioto / México / 2026 Un fotógrafo de sucesos se ve envuelto con un agente secreto después de que se encuentre un cadáver dentro de una maleta.

El bosque salvaje Wildwood (Wildwood) / Dir. Travis Knight / EE. UU., Reino Unido, Canadá / 2026 Las aventuras de Prue McKeel mientras se adentra en los bosques a las afueras de Portland para encontrar a su hermano secuestrado.

Entrega al límite (Runner) / Dir. Scott Waugh / Australia, EE. UU., Reino Unido / 2026 Un exsoldado y su improbable compañero se convierten en el objetivo de un cártel despiadado mientras corren para completar un parto médico crítico y salvar la vida de una niña.

El desconocido del gran arco (L’inconnu de la Grande Arche) / Dir. Stéphane Demoustier / Francia, Dinamarca / 2026 La historia de Otto von Spreckelsen, un profesor de arquitectura de la vida real originario de Copenhague, que sorprendió al mundo al ganar un concurso abierto convocado por el presidente francés François Mitterrand.

Campeón gabacho / Dir. Jonás Cuarón / México / 2026 Un migrante mexicano decidido se abre camino a través de los desafíos y la discriminación en Estados Unidos, utilizando su espíritu de lucha y optimismo para superar la adversidad y encontrar un éxito inesperado.

Everest: The Other Side / Dirs. Jimmy Chin, Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi / EE. UU. / 2026 Los alpinistas de élite Jim Morrison y Hilaree Nelson intentan escalar y esquiar la cara norte directa del Monte Everest, el descenso de esquí más peligroso y codiciado del planeta.

También te podría interesar: Cartelera de Cinépolis – Estrenos de esta semana .

Cartelera Cinemex: películas que aún puedes encontrar

La isla de las muñecas / Dir. Homero McDonald Chávez / México / 2026

Street Fighter / Dir. Kitao Sakurai / EE. UU., Japón / 2026

Súper canino (Charlie the Wonderdog) / Dir. Shea Wageman / EE. UU. / 2026

El final (It Ends) / Dir. Alexander Ullom / EE. UU. / 2025

Hope, el primer impacto (Hope) / Dir. Na Hong-jin / Corea del Sur / 2026

Shaun el cordero: el monstruo de Mossy Bottom (Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom) / Dirs. Steve Cox, Matthew Walker / Francia, Reino Unido, EE. UU. / 2026

¿Qué llegará la próxima semana a la cartelera Cinemex (jueves 29 de octubre 2026)?

Caballo salvaje nueve (Wild Horse Nine) / Dir. Martin McDonagh / Reino Unido, EE. UU., Chile / 2026

Gozilla menos cero (Godzilla Minus Zero) / Dir. Takashi Yamazaki / Japón / 2026 La familia Shikishima se enfrenta a una amenaza completamente nueva con el regreso de Godzilla, que sembrará el caos.

Klara y el sol (Klara and the Sun) / Dir. Taika Waititi / Reino Unido, India, EE. UU. / 2026 Una niña robot diseñada para prevenir la soledad intenta salvar a una familia de humanos desconsolada.

El gato con sombrero (The Cat in the Hat) / Dirs. Alessandro Carloni, Erica Rivinoja / EE. UU. / 2026 El gato con sombrero se enfrenta a su misión más difícil hasta ahora para el I.I.I.I. (Instituto para la Institución de la Imaginación e Inspiración, S.A.): animar a Gabby y Sebastián, dos hermanos que están teniendo dificultades para adaptarse a su nueva ciudad. Conocido por siempre llevar las cosas al extremo, esta podría ser la última oportunidad de este agente del caos para demostrar su valía… o perder su sombrero mágico.

Grin, el juego de la oiuja (Grin) / Dir. Lawrence Fowler / Reino Unido / 2026 Eva visita a su familia y conoce a Lucian, la nueva pareja de su madre, quien le presenta un inquietante juego de mesa antiguo. Lo que comienza como un juego divertido se torna mortal cuando desata una entidad demoníaca que persigue a los jugadores con oscuros secretos, haciéndolos desaparecer uno a uno.

Caballo salvaje nueve (Wild Horse Nine) / Dir. Martin McDonagh / Reino Unido, EE. UU., Chile / 2026 Los agentes de la CIA Chris y Lee se enfrentan a una misión de prueba de confianza desde Santiago hasta la Isla de Pascua durante 1973 en Chile.

La venus eléctrica (La Vénus électrique) / Dir. Pierre Salvadori / Francia, Bélgica / 2026 En el París de 1928, un pintor, incapaz de trabajar desde la muerte de su esposa, participa sin saberlo en falsos espectáculos espiritistas organizados por un feriante. A medida que recupera la inspiración, ella se enamora del hombre al que está engañando.

Rocky – 50 aniversario (Rocky) – reestreno / Dir. John G. Avildsen / EE. UU. / 2026 Un boxeador de poca monta de Filadelfia tiene una oportunidad sumamente excepcional de enfrentarse al campeón mundial de peso pesado en un combate en el que luchará por llegar hasta el final para preservar su dignidad.

article_text:
Week in wildlife: a penguin posse, a little leopard cat and a chonky squirrel

This week’s best wildlife photographs from around the world

Fri 16 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT

Wildlife Photographer of the Year award . Elliott opens a window into the lives of the often-misunderstood coyotes living in the environs of San Francisco. About 100 of these urban-adapted wild canines live alongside more than 800,000 human inhabitants, and attitudes towards them are mixed. Coyotes sometimes prey on domestic animals, but they also bring benefits such as controlling disease-carrying rodentsPhotograph: Loren Elliott/PA

freshwater turtle is one of 13 that are being returned to their home, the Gingham water hole in New South Wales, Australia, which dried up after the water company cut flows to the area. After a public outcry, the utility reversed its decision, and 24 more turtles will soon follow the first group of 13 back to their restored habitatPhotograph: NSW Government

article_text:
写真家YUTARO SAITOによる展覧会「72 CLUB TOUR」が、2026年9月18日から10月2日まで、東京・板橋のCOPY CENTER GALLERYで開催されている。

SAITOは2021年より、「NOT PLASTIC FASHION」をコンセプトに高齢者のファッションを撮影してきた。衣服がイメージとして大量に流通する現代において、彼がカメラを向けるのは、その背後にある身体と個人の時間だ。高齢者の装いを通して、「着る」という日常的な行為のなかに蓄積された記憶や習慣を掘り起こしている。

本展は、新たに刊行される写真集『72 CLUB CALENDAR』に合わせ、国内主要ブックフェアでの販売と全国各地での展示を行う巡回プロジェクト。同書は、これまでNOTEやFASHIONSNAPなどで発表してきた高齢男性へのファッションインタビューに、未発表作品を加えて再構成したものだ。

特徴的なのは、高齢者の装いが持つ「機能性」に着目していること。『72 CLUB CALENDAR』自体も、一般的な写真集にとどまらず、カレンダーであり、写真集であり、さらには展示物でもあるという複数の機能を併せ持つ。本展では同書とともに、高齢男性を写したポートレート作品や衣服、「NOT PLASTIC FASHION(2030)」シリーズからポスター作品を展示する。

流行や新しさが絶えず更新されるファッションの世界に対し、長い年月をかけて身体になじみ、生活の一部となった服は何を物語るのか。SAITOの写真は、装うことを表層的なスタイルとしてではなく、一人ひとりが生きてきた時間や身体の記録として捉え直している。

タイトル

YUTARO SAITO「72 CLUB TOUR」

場所

COPY CENTER GALLERY（東京都板橋区板橋4-4-2 ミクニビル1F／B1F）

会期

2026年9月18日（金）〜10月2日（金）

時間

13:00〜19:00

休み

無し

料金

500円

URL

https://www.instagram.com/yutarosaito/?hl=ja

In these images, his eye carries what his publisher calls “the dual inheritance of two formative disciplines”: “a surfer’s responsiveness to shifting conditions”."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/colin-dodgson-lj04.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Colin Dodgson 2026 courtesy Loose Joints", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/colin-dodgson-lj16.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Colin Dodgson 2026 courtesy Loose Joints", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/colin-dodgson-lj01.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Colin Dodgson 2026 courtesy Loose Joints", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Earthquake Weather dances along the faultlines between typology and sprawl: thumbed, dog-eared book pages worn soft by use; contemporary memento mori that turn to the flesh and its impermanence; plastic water bottles left on Japanese roadsides. The tenor of an uncertain age seeps in, uncommented upon, by simple contiguity."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/colin-dodgson-lj09.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Colin Dodgson 2026 courtesy Loose Joints", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/colin-dodgson-lj11.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Colin Dodgson 2026 courtesy Loose Joints", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/colin-dodgson-lj10.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Colin Dodgson 2026 courtesy Loose Joints", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What organizes Earthquake Weather is accumulation — not as rhetorical device, but as condition of the world. With Earthquake Weathe r, his debut monograph published by Loose Joints, the American photographer casts fragility, mortality and the everyday as allegories of a saturated world.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Colin Dodgson.

When he is not shooting campaigns for Dior, Gucci and Louis Vuitton in Vogue , W Magazine or The New York Times Style Magazine , Colin Dodgson pursues a photography entirely his own, printing his work by hand in the darkroom. In these images, his eye carries what his publisher calls “the dual inheritance of two formative disciplines”: “a surfer’s responsiveness to shifting conditions”.

Earthquake Weather dances along the faultlines between typology and sprawl: thumbed, dog-eared book pages worn soft by use; contemporary memento mori that turn to the flesh and its impermanence; plastic water bottles left on Japanese roadsides. So many figures of a precarious existence, gathered without hierarchy or imposed narrative, in burnished, copper tones.

Without warning, the sequence drifts towards a darker register. Fentanyl bottles appear, lined neatly in a row. Atmospheric CO2 readings insert themselves between the silhouettes and the worn books, alongside extracts from his collaborations with the World Land Trust — a British charity dedicated to protecting threatened natural habitats — across areas of ecological importance. The tenor of an uncertain age seeps in, uncommented upon, by simple contiguity.

What organizes Earthquake Weather is accumulation — not as rhetorical device, but as condition of the world. The book explores “the way we accumulate: in knowledge, within our bodies, through consumption, against entropy.” The images work as fugues, reacting across the page: beauty and ruin coexist.

Dodgson’s photography chases what “both hides and reveals itself within the same blink of an eye.” He has slipped into its pages photographs of volumes leafed through and annotated — and his own book might follow suit, becoming, through use, one of the photographs it contains.

Earthquake Weather by Colin Dodgson is published by Loose Joints , edited by Sarah Chaplin Espenon. 88 pages, 60 colour plates. €46.

article_text:
‘I could never be Satan’s boy. I haven’t the humility.” The speaker is Father Urbain Grandier, the 17th-century French priest accused of witchcraft, stylishly played by Oliver Reed, in Ken Russell’s scabrous 1971 classic; it is now restored and rereleased in its complete form after years of censorship. It comes from an era when movies, playing in high-street cinemas, still had the power to shock, to position that shock in the polite cultural mainstream and to compel serious discussion about whether that shock – or, conversely, a ban – was justified.

The Devils is based on a true story of politically directed mass hysteria, adapted by Russell from two literary works: Aldous Huxley’s The Devils of Loudun and John Whiting’s stage play The Devils . Of course it is obscene; obscenity is the glowing sulphurous paint which Russell is applying to the canvas. It is about obscenity – but the obscenity does not reside in the sexualised images of the crucified Christ or naked nuns disporting themselves; it is the violence of authority that is shown to be obscene. The idea of martyrs or heretics being burned at the stake has long been an accepted fact recounted in U-certificate history lessons, and a punishment which survived well into the European enlightenment. Russell shows you what it might actually look like and that is to involve a confrontational assault on good taste.

Reed is a revelation with his intelligent, focused, charismatic and dignified performance as the sensualist cleric who submits to injustice like a dissolute version of Thomas Becket. Grandier is a magnetically handsome man and de facto municipal leader of the town of Loudun in western France, bullishly promoting its independence, its walls and fortifications; this is to the rage of Cardinal Richelieu (Christopher Logue) and the Catholic church, who suspect that it will become a sanctuary and power-base for Huguenots and Protestants.

Grandier is blandly tolerated by the equally decadent and vain Louis XIII (Graham Armitage); the king’s bizarre court masque is shown in the film’s stunning opening scene, with superb music by Peter Maxwell Davies, whose compositions do so much to give this film its crazed, dissonant fervour. Loudun’s Ursuline abbess Sister Jeanne Des Anges, played with radioactive certainty by Vanessa Redgrave , is sexually frustrated like more or less every authority figure here – the displacement of sexuality into tyranny is, after all, part of the point – and tormented by her spinal-curvature disability; she is infatuated by Grandier and enraged by him marrying another woman, Madeline De Brou (played by Gemma Jones), and moreover declining her offer to be the order’s father confessor.

So Sister Jeanne spitefully invents stories about his demonic hold over everyone, a tale cynically seized upon by cynical agents of the state, who then fan the flames of hysteria – although Russell does not entirely endorse the theory that the nuns were themselves cynically putting on a show to incriminate Grandier. The priest’s persecutors are Baron de Laubardemont (Dudley Sutton) and the order’s Father-Canon Jean Mignon (Murray Melvin), a thin-faced disapproving ascetic who is to become this story’s contrite and despairing Judas to Grandier’s Jesus.

Russell allows us now to register what was perhaps not registered fully in 1971: the misogyny behind the publicising of her deformity over the centuries, turning it into a mark of villainy like that of Shakespeare’s Richard III, exaggerated or even invented by posterity’s myth-making. It is part of a tradition of monstrosity – perhaps even inaugurated by the self-flagellating abbess herself – that dramatised the penitent view that a woman’s sexuality was an ugly disorderly phenomenon.

As well as everything else, The Devils is also about fascism; like upmarket psycho-sexual shockers of the same era such as Visconti’s The Damned in 1969, Cavani’s The Night Porter from 1974, or Pasolini’s Salò from 1975, it sees power licensing and permitting sexual decadence as a safety valve for discontented, frustrated energies that might otherwise be directed against the state. Yet it also uses that decadence as a pretext for moral panic and cracking down, and even rechannelling the mad sexual excitement into power worship.

What comes across in the film is the cynicism of the religious authorities whose officers are quite well aware of more modern concepts of frustration and hysteria. Simply and importantly, the possessions and the “devils” are not real, or not real in the sense they are held to be by the church. How intriguing that just two years later, in Friedkin’s The Exorcist, we were offered a story of authentic possession, a plausibly conceived possession whose metaphorical properties can only be absorbed at one remove.

The amazing, anachronistic set designs of the young Derek Jarman present to us the white-tiled nunnery, whose low arched ceilings mean everyone has to duck down in imitation of the abbess; it looks like a Victorian or Edwardian prison or public lavatory, while the giant, multi-storied library looks like the jailhouse in which Elvis Presley sang. The great brickwork walls of the city make it resemble the housing estate in Kubrick’s Clockwork Orange, released in the same year – and in fact Grandier’s torture scene is very Clockwork Orange.

When the devils depart and the fever abates, what is left behind is a scorched and desolate landscape, like that after a plague or an apocalypse: a chilling final flourish to Ken Russell’s aria of angry pessimism.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 我们今年庆祝摄影诞生200周年，为此已经出版了各种各样的出版物。娜塔莉·赫施多弗（Nathalie Herschdorfer）的这本新书在其中独树一帜，它汇集了200幅精选的、对其时代具有代表性的纪实与艺术影像……

"paragraph", "text": "今年人们在庆祝尼谢福尔·涅普斯（Nicéphore Niépce）拍摄的第一张照片问世200周年——这是一张传奇般的影像，他在圣卢德瓦朗讷（St-Loup-de-Varennes）的住所窗户前，用感光沥青层经过八小时的曝光拍摄而成。虽然这创造了第一张永久保存的相机影像，但涅普斯的方法几乎还不适合实际应用。直到13年后，路易·达盖尔（Louis Daguerre）的方法才被公之于众，并于1839年被法国政府作为礼物赠予全世界。在此之前的几十年里，将暗箱影像定格下来可以说是“空气中弥漫的想法”，因为在许多国家都有成功的实验者，他们或多或少成功地使用了各种不同的物质做到了这一点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "娜塔莉·赫施多弗（Nathalie Herschdorfer）的书以涅普斯的第一张照片为契机，重新梳理了从过去到当代的摄影史。但这不仅仅是一部全新的摄影史：赫施多弗给自己设定了一个具有挑战性的任务，即为这二百年中的每一年挑选出一张典型照片，将其呈现在整页或跨页上，并用简短的文字进行描述。因此，这并非一本传统意义上的历史书，而是一次经过策展的、贯穿200年摄影图像文化的旅程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "显而易见，这样的大胆尝试极具挑战性，且不可避免地带有主观色彩，因为正是在当代摄影中，这种评估比在早期时代要困难得多。凭借其在勒洛克勒美术馆（Kunstmuseum Le Locle）以及后来的爱丽舍博物馆（Musée Elysée）的学习经历和以往工作，娜塔莉·赫施多弗（Nathalie Herschdorfer）天生就适合挑选出各年份的“偶像级”作品。尽管如此，这种方法并非没有问题，因为谁若想在320页的篇幅中呈现200年的摄影史，就必须做出激进的选择。每一次选择都会产生侧重点和遗漏。正对于精通摄影史的读者而言，不仅赫施多弗展示的内容引人入胜，她没有展示的内容以及她将哪些事件宣布为里程碑同样引人入胜。“每个人都是通过自己经验的过滤器来看待一张照片，因此感知到的是完全不同的东西，”作者在前言中坦言，“事实上，我们只看到我们想看的东西。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "娜塔莉·赫施多弗（Nathalie Herschdorfer）将这200年划分为六个时代：从先驱者、摄影新闻的诞生、摄影作为艺术的日益认可，到实验、颠覆以及数字时代。每个章节前都有一条记录重要事件的时间轴。11篇专题文章深入探讨了各个时代和思潮。其中，摄影史上的重要之声也得以发表，例如纳达尔（Nadar）1857年的陈述，或露西亚·莫霍利（Lucia Moholy）1939年发表的文章《摄影100年》（«100 Jahre Fotografie»）的摘录，并辅以多位特邀作者的撰稿。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管赫施多弗是一名策展人，但她并未将摄影仅仅视为一种艺术形式。这本书介于技术史、艺术史、纪实摄影、新闻与社会史以及日常生活文化之间。这恰恰是它的优势所在：摄影呈现为一种不仅产出图像、更改变了我们对世界感知的媒介。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这本书适合谁？与其说它是一本关于摄影史的参考书，不如说它是一幅经过精心策划的全景图，展现了摄影在200年里如何改变了我们的世界和我们的视觉。这样一本书的质量不取决于其完整性，而取决于其选择的智慧。正是因为这种选择具有主观性，这本书才为摄影史的鉴赏家们提供了丰富的素材，供他们去发现、赞同——以及偶尔产生异议。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph",
